walkthrough:
See the Shared Pattern First**
Both curves rise to a peak and then fall. That is the normal enzyme temperature curve - increasing kinetic energy speeds up reaction, then loss of activase function at high temperature reduces activity. Both also meet at about $30^{\circ}\text{C}$ with activity about 0.104 arbitrary units.

Compare the Optima and Peaks**
False flax (open circles) peaks earlier and higher, at about $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ with about 0.117-0.118 au. Cotton (closed circles) peaks later and lower, at about $30^{\circ}\text{C}$ with about 0.103-0.104 au. So cotton has the higher optimum temperature, false flax has the higher maximum activity.

Compare Below and Above the Crossover**
Because they cross at $30^{\circ}\text{C}$, you can split the comparison. For example at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ false flax is ~0.112 au while cotton is ~0.098 au. At $35^{\circ}\text{C}$ the reverse is true - cotton is ~0.093 au while false flax is only ~0.050 au. Always quote paired values with units.

Compare Temperature Range**
Cotton activase keeps working at higher temperatures. False flax activity falls to near zero by ~$37.5^{\circ}\text{C}$, while cotton still shows activity up to ~$42.5^{\circ}\text{C}$. In a compare answer give both similarities and differences with numbers.

Final answer: Cotton has higher optimum temp ~$30^{\circ}\text{C}$ vs false flax ~$25^{\circ}\text{C}$; peak activity higher in false flax ~0.118 au vs cotton ~0.104 au; below $30^{\circ}\text{C}$ false flax has higher activity, above $30^{\circ}\text{C}$ cotton has higher activity; cotton works up to ~$42.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ vs false flax only to ~$37.5^{\circ}\text{C}$; both increase then decrease; both ~0.104 au at $30^{\circ}\text{C}$. Any four.

hints: Think about where in the world a plant like cotton grows compared to false flax - what selection pressure would temperature create?
Remember that every enzyme is coded for by DNA - what must be different in the DNA of the two species to make a different enzyme?
Link that DNA difference to protein shape - which levels of protein structure determine how an enzyme behaves at high temperature?
walkthrough:
Link to Habitat and Adaptation**
Cotton grows in hotter parts of the world than false flax. Natural selection has favoured cotton plants whose activase still works when leaves get hot, while false flax is adapted to cooler conditions.

From Genes to Amino Acids**
The two species have different genes / alleles coding for rubisco activase. That means a different sequence of amino acids is assembled - a different primary structure.

From Primary to Tertiary Structure**
A different amino acid sequence folds into a slightly different tertiary structure with different hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions. The cotton form holds its active shape at higher temperatures, so its optimum is shifted to the right.

Final answer: Cotton adapted to / lives in higher temperature areas; different genes / alleles for rubisco activase in cotton vs flax; gives different primary structure / amino acid sequence; gives different tertiary structure / 3D shape / bonds, so different thermal stability.

hints: Recall the very first step of the Calvin cycle in the stroma - what two substrates does rubisco join together?
If that first product is not made, follow the cycle forward - what happens to production of GP, TP and then glucose?
Now follow the cycle around in a loop - what happens to regeneration of the starting acceptor if the cycle slows or stops?
walkthrough:
Stop Carbon Fixation**
Rubisco catalyses $CO_2$ + RuBP $\rightarrow$ 2 x GP. Denaturation means the active site loses its specific 3D shape, so RuBP and $CO_2$ can no longer bind. Carboxylation stops.

Starve the Rest of the Cycle**
With no GP made, there is less GP reduced to TP using ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent reactions. So less TP is available to make glucose, amino acids, lipids and other products.

Break the Cycle**
Normally some TP is used to regenerate RuBP using ATP. With less TP, less RuBP is regenerated, so even if some rubisco remained, there would be less acceptor to fix $CO_2$. The whole Calvin cycle slows and then stops.
Final answer: Less / no carboxylation of RuBP / $CO_2$ fixation; less / no GP converted to TP; less / no regeneration of RuBP; less / no glucose / hexose made.

walkthrough:
Borrow the Heat-Stable Gene**
Fig. 2.1 shows cotton activase still works at $35-42.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ when false flax activase has almost stopped. Take the gene / cDNA coding for cotton rubisco activase and insert it into false flax or another crop plant embryo.

Explain the Benefit**
The transgenic plant will make heat-stable activase, so rubisco stays active at high environmental temperatures. Carbon fixation, Calvin cycle and glucose production can continue, giving growth and good yield when hot.

Final answer: Take gene / cDNA for cotton rubisco activase and insert into false flax / crop plant; to maintain rubisco activity at high temperatures / above $37.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ / up to $42.5^{\circ}\text{C}$, so Calvin cycle / photosynthesis continues.
